source.title: Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
source.authors: Ivan Lee; Nan-Jiang Jiang; Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick

page_placements.theme: Data structure, depth and architecture set ICL emergence and in-context loss profiles in small models

record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests the training-data-dependence part of V5 by varying burstiness and observing in-context learning in synthetic image classification. It does not identify or manipulate induction heads.
record.gate_note: The study reports ICL outcomes under different burstiness conditions and reports training-step timing for some of those outcomes. Its language-modeling ICL-score results do not measure induction-head formation or establish its timing relative to an ICL gain or loss bump. The synthetic-task accuracy results do not identify the mechanism behind ICL.
record.test_reason: The study measures in-context learning (ICL) accuracy and ICL score across 13 architectures trained from scratch. It never identifies, ablates or times induction heads or previous-token heads. Its burstiness results show the training data controls whether ICL emerges (Chan et al.'s result), not whether induction heads form or whether ICL persists, so they measure a related construct rather than V5. Its abrupt ICL-score gains in non-attention models are measured without any induction-head or loss-bump measure, so they do not test V2. Its associative-recall success in non-attention models shows induction-like behaviour, not heads, so it does not test V4. Induction heads appear only in the authors' discussion of Olsson et al. These findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right but incomplete. The headline conclusion is that all considered architectures can perform ICL, and that some attention alternatives match or beat transformers. No architecture is consistent beyond the training prompt lengths. Burstiness and architecture affect predisposition toward ICL versus memorization. The authors note abrupt ICL-score gains across most architectures and ask what mechanism analogous to induction heads serves this role in head-less models. They do not test induction heads themselves.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains diverse architectures from scratch on synthetic ICL tasks and varies training-data burstiness; it does not use the original induction-head identification or mechanistic analysis method.
record.method_sensitivity: Image-classification ICL outcomes vary with P(bursty), architecture, and training run; RetNet emergence was rare and late, while the best-run result differed from average performance for some architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: ICL in Omniglot image classification is absent with non-bursty training and emerges at architecture-dependent burstiness levels. Some architectures (RetNet, S4, CNNs, RNNs) favour memorization on average at P(bursty)=1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether ICL (not induction heads specifically) emerges depends on training-data burstiness and on architecture, including non-attention architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: ICL emergence timing in the image task differs by architecture: RetNet and the RNNs emerge after ~30K steps, while the other high performers emerge in under 10K steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The training step at which ICL emerges varies by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: On TinyStories language modeling, most architectures, including ones without attention heads, show an abrupt improvement in ICL score (Section 6, Figure 3). Image-task ICL emerges in the same window.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An abrupt ICL-score transition occurs in architectures that have no attention heads, so the transition does not require induction heads.

fits_no_version.finding: All 13 architectures, including RNNs, CNNs and SSMs, solve associative recall in context (Section 4, Figure 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction-like key-value copying behaviour is achievable without attention heads.

record.problems: The induction-head mechanism is not measured. Image-classification outcomes depend on architecture and hyperparameter/run selection; the authors attribute some RNN results to luck. Numerical plotted accuracies and uncertainty intervals are not stated in the text provided.
record.rows_left_out: Exact plotted values and per-run/model sweep results in Figures 2 and 8 and Tables 13-14 were not separately extracted; the supplied table text contains no readable entries for those values. Other task results are not rows because they do not test induction heads or the data-dependence result captured by V5.

untested.parts: No previous-token heads, head composition or [A][B]…[A]→[B] circuit analysis.
ICL-score jumps reported, but no induction-head formation or loss-bump measurement.
No attribution of ICL to induction heads in any model; only small (~33M) models are trained.
No heads with induction behaviour identified in any architecture.
Burstiness is varied, but its effect on induction-head formation or timing, and on ICL persistence, is not measured.
No comparison of induction heads with other mechanisms for few-shot learning.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'tests' guess is rejected: V5 concerns induction-head formation and ICL persistence, and the study measures only ICL emergence. The abrupt ICL-score gains in non-attention models (Figure 3) are the most relevant finding for this phenomenon but have no rows. A future version about whether ICL phase changes require induction heads could use them. Appendix F mentions ICL decay in transformers in the image task, but this is unquantified.

versions.untested_parts: Does not inspect previous-token heads, head composition, or the [A][B] … [A] → [B] mechanism.
Reports ICL-score trajectories, but does not measure induction-head formation or establish that it coincides with ICL-score change and a training-loss bump.
Does not measure whether induction heads carry most ICL in large transformers.
Tests ICL in diverse architectures, but not heads with induction behaviour across families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Tests how burstiness and architecture relate to ICL outcomes, including some emergence timing. Does not test induction-head formation or whether induction heads' formation depends on data or setup.
Does not compare induction heads with other mechanisms as carriers of few-shot task learning.
Does not resolve whether induction-head formation comprises multiple sub-steps or transitions.

relation.reason: Section 6 discusses Olsson et al.'s induction-head explanation and asks what analogous mechanisms might exist in alternative architectures; it does not investigate those mechanisms.

tranche.reason: The study measures task ICL and language-model ICL scores, without identifying induction heads, measuring their formation, or testing their causal contribution. These are related constructs rather than tests of the listed versions.

source_check.notes: The extracted tables contain captions without cells, but the prose supports all listed qualitative values and timing bounds. The study measures ICL emergence, not induction-head formation or persistence of ICL during continued training.

statements.correction: Omniglot: no evaluated architecture demonstrates ICL with purely non-bursty training. ICL preference varies with architecture and burstiness. RetNet: ICL in only 2 of 108 runs, after 30K training steps. Three RNNs: emergence in a similar window. Other high-performing architectures from Section 4: fewer than 10K steps. LightConv: no image-classification ICL even in the best-run analysis.
statements.problem: The burstiness findings and under-10K comparison are supported, but approximately 30K changes RetNet's stated timing from a lower bound to an approximate point.
